title: Determinism and float
sub: FloatMode, FloatPrecision, FMA, and what is actually guaranteed when two clients must compute the same thing
cards/0/title: The order of operations changes the result
cards/0/body:
float addition isn’t associative: (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can differ in the last bits, and sometimes by a lot. In the example, 1e8f + 1f rounds back to 1e8f and the one is lost — in the other order it survives.

Hence the sources of divergence that come up in interviews:

Reordering. A vectorized sum is 8 partial sums added at the end, which is a different order.

FMA — multiply and add in one instruction, with one rounding instead of two.

Different function implementations: sin, exp and pow are approximated differently in different libraries and instruction sets.

For graphics this doesn’t matter. It matters where two machines must get the same bits: a lockstep multiplayer game, input-based replays, anti-cheat by recomputation.
cards/1/body:
FMA (fused multiply-add) computes a * b + c in one instruction and rounds once. That is more accurate than multiplying, rounding, adding and rounding again. But the bits come out different.

So FMA is a problem of agreement, not accuracy: if one machine’s compiler fused the operation and another’s didn’t (another CPU, another code variant, another mode), the results diverge. Over thousands of simulation steps, a difference in the last bit turns into a unit standing somewhere else.

In Burst, fusing into FMA is allowed by FloatMode.Fast. Unity.Mathematics has math.mad(a, b, c), and its documentation says outright that with fast math on some architectures it may become an FMA.
cards/2/body:
FloatMode is set in [BurstCompile] and says what liberties with float the compiler may take.

Default is the same as Strict: no reordering, denormals and NaN are respected.

Fast allows algebraically equivalent reordering, multiplying by a reciprocal instead of dividing, and FMA; the compiler may assume there are no NaNs or infinities. Faster, but the result may differ from Strict.

Deterministic gives the same result on all supported platforms. It works since Burst 1.8.25; before that the value was reserved and did nothing. 64-bit architectures only. Burst turns off the optimizations that cause platform differences and flushes subnormals to zero everywhere; identical NaN bits are not promised, and speed may drop.

The mode can be set per job, for a whole assembly with [assembly: BurstCompile(...)], and the Burst AOT settings have a default Floating Point Mode.
cards/3/q: A job that sums forces was given FloatMode.Fast. The result now differs from before in the last digits. What is it?
cards/3/options/0: Expected behaviour: Fast allows reordering and fusing into FMA, hence different last bits
cards/3/options/1: A Burst bug — roll back the package version
cards/3/options/2: A data race between worker threads
cards/3/options/3: In Fast mode Burst computes in half instead of float
cards/3/explain: Fast changes the order of the computation and may fuse a multiply with an add — mathematically the same result, but different bits. If the bits themselves matter, you don’t use Fast.
cards/3/wrong/1: This is the documented behaviour of the mode, not a compiler bug.
cards/3/wrong/2: A race would give results that jump around, not consistently different ones; besides, the float mode has nothing to do with threads.
cards/3/wrong/3: Fast doesn’t change the type: a float stays 32-bit. What changes is the order of operations and how they’re fused.
cards/4/body:
FloatPrecision is a separate knob: how accurately Burst computes math.sin, math.cos, math.exp, math.log, math.pow and the like. Accuracy is measured in ulp (unit in the last place) — the distance between neighbouring floats of that magnitude.

Standard is the default and the same as Medium: 3.5 ulp. High is 1 ulp. Low is up to 350 ulp for sin, cos, exp, log, pow, fmod and their variants; other functions are as in Medium.

Don’t mix them up: FloatPrecision is about accuracy, FloatMode is about freedom to reorder and agreement of results. High doesn’t make code deterministic, and Low is a fair choice for waves, particles and other effects where nobody will see an error in the third digit.
cards/5/q: Match the setting to what it does
cards/5/pairs/0/1: No reordering; NaN and denormals respected
cards/5/pairs/2/1: The same result on all 64-bit platforms
cards/5/pairs/3/1: sin, exp, pow with an error of up to 350 ulp
cards/6/title: What is guaranteed and what isn’t
cards/6/body:
Essentially one thing is guaranteed: the same code, the same inputs, the same order, the same build on the same CPU — the same bits from run to run.

Not promised in Strict or Fast: the same result on x64 and ARM64; on two x64 machines, if Burst picked different code variants for them (SSE4 and AVX2); between Burst and Mono/IL2CPP for the same formula.

Deterministic covers platforms, but only for Burst code. If the float inputs came from managed code, or Burst calls a function pointer compiled without Deterministic, the guarantee breaks.

The order is your job in any mode. If a parallel job writes into a queue through a ParallelWriter, the element order depends on which thread got there first — and a sum in another order is another sum. For determinism, the data is sorted or written to fixed indices, and summed in one order.
cards/7/q: A lockstep game with the simulation in Burst. What can make two clients diverge? Pick all that apply.
cards/7/options/1: A float sum over elements a parallel job wrote through a ParallelWriter, in arrival order
cards/7/options/2: Part of a formula computed in a MonoBehaviour and part in Burst, with clients on different platforms
cards/7/options/3: Integer arithmetic in a fixed order
cards/7/options/4: FloatMode.Deterministic on 64-bit clients with the same inputs and order
cards/7/explain: Fast reorders and fuses into FMA differently on different machines. The arrival order from a ParallelWriter changes from run to run, and the float sum changes with it. Deterministic doesn’t cover managed code, and its floats on different platforms don’t have to agree. Integers in a fixed order agree everywhere, and Deterministic with the same inputs and order is exactly the case the mode was made for.
cards/8/body:
The classic answer for lockstep is fixed point: a number is stored as an integer multiplied by a constant factor. In 16.16 format the value 1.5 is stored as 98304 (1.5 × 65536). Addition is an integer add, multiplication goes through a long and a shift.

Integer arithmetic gives the same bits everywhere: on x64 and ARM, in 32 and 64 bits, in Burst and in Mono. That’s why many lockstep RTS games are built this way.

The price: a narrow range (16.16 is about ±32,768) and overflow you have to keep in mind; your own sqrt, sin and tables; longer code that is slower to write. And everything Unity computes for you in float (physics, animation) can’t be part of the simulation.

FloatMode.Deterministic is a newer alternative if all clients are 64-bit and the whole simulation runs in Burst.
cards/9/q: A lockstep RTS: clients on Windows x64, Android ARM64 and old 32-bit Android. The simulation is in Burst. What do you pick for the simulation numbers?
cards/9/options/0: Fixed point on integers: the same bits on every client, 32-bit ones included
cards/9/options/2: FloatMode.Strict: it reorders nothing, so the results will match
cards/9/options/3: FloatPrecision.High: at 1 ulp there will be no divergence
cards/9/explain: Deterministic is supported only on 64-bit architectures, and the list has 32-bit clients. Strict doesn’t reorder operations, but doesn’t promise agreement across platforms. That leaves integers.
cards/9/wrong/1: Deterministic is 64-bit only. The 32-bit Android clients aren’t covered.
cards/9/wrong/2: Strict removes reordering, but not the differences between platforms and function implementations.
cards/9/wrong/3: FloatPrecision is about function accuracy, not agreement: a 1 ulp error that differs between machines is already a divergence.
cards/10/task: Set the modes. ParticleJob is visual sparks: give it FloatMode.Fast and FloatPrecision.Low. SimStepJob is a lockstep simulation step, and all clients are 64-bit: give it FloatMode.Deterministic. No bare [BurstCompile] without parameters may remain.
cards/10/checks/3/label: Neither job is left with a parameterless [BurstCompile]
cards/10/explain: Nobody compares sparks bit by bit, so they may have both reordering and rough functions. The simulation must agree on every client, so it gets Deterministic (Burst 1.8.25+, 64-bit), and the inputs and processing order must be the same everywhere. Both ways of writing it, the constructor (FloatPrecision.Low, FloatMode.Fast) and FloatMode = ..., are equally valid.
cards/11/q: Interviewer: “Why not just turn on FloatMode.Deterministic for the whole assembly, to be safe?”
cards/11/options/0: It turns off some float optimizations and can slow the code down; it’s only needed where results must agree between machines
cards/11/options/1: Because Deterministic is reserved and does nothing
cards/11/explain: Determinism is paid for in speed: Burst gives up the optimizations that cause platform differences. It’s enabled selectively — for the simulation, replays, server-side verification — while rendering, particles and animation stay on Default or Fast.
cards/11/wrong/1: That was true before Burst 1.8.25. Since that version Deterministic is supported (on 64-bit platforms).
cards/11/wrong/2: The float mode applies to the compiled code and doesn’t depend on the job type.
